_note: One-line headlines for the 28 dataset findings (22 Oct 2026), written from the full finding text. Full figures, methods and limitations stay in the other columns.

headline.D01: All 5,175 EPFL questions from 54 courses are graded and usable
headline.D02: In one attempt, GPT-4 fully answered almost half (46.7%) of computer science questions
headline.D03: With the best of 8 prompts, GPT-4 fully answered 85.6% of computer science questions
headline.D04: On multiple-choice questions GPT-4 scored about twice what guessing would (52.2% vs 26.5%)
headline.D05: GPT-4 did about as well on open-answer questions as on multiple choice
headline.D06: GPT-4 clearly outperformed GPT-3.5, so newer models are likely stronger still
headline.D07: How the question is prompted changed GPT-4's multiple-choice grade by up to 15 points
headline.D08: GPT-4 passed the 0.5 mark in 13 of 17 computer science courses on its first attempt
headline.D09: Master's-level questions were no harder for GPT-4 than Bachelor's-level ones
headline.D10: GPT-4 performed similarly on English and French questions
headline.D11: Questions containing code and longer multiple-choice questions were somewhat harder for GPT-4
headline.D12: Almost all capstone students (92.7%) used generative AI in their project
headline.D13: Students mostly used AI for code and learning, rarely for design or requirements
headline.D14: Students used general chatbots far more than the university-hosted tool (74.7% vs 5.3%)
headline.D15: Students used AI both to propose solutions and to review their own, about equally
headline.D16: Heavier AI use went with letting AI propose solutions first
headline.D17: Self-rated programming skill did not clearly change how much students used AI
headline.D18: Most students (64.0%) found AI use in the project useful; 12.7% found it harmful
headline.D19: Students' most common advice to peers was to keep their own understanding
headline.D20: Clients worried most about students' independent understanding, yet most wanted AI use encouraged
headline.D21: StudyChat covers 16,851 prompts from 203 students; 175 have both chats and grades
headline.D22: Students mostly asked the AI to explain (47.1%) rather than to write or edit (31.2%)
headline.D23: Chats opened about equally with a writing request or a conceptual question
headline.D24: 90.6% of students scored higher on AI-permitted assignments than on supervised exams
headline.D25: Assignment marks bunched near full marks, so they barely separated students
headline.D26: How students used the chatbot did not predict their marks or the assignment-exam gap
headline.D27: Using the chatbot on an assignment made no clear difference to its mark
headline.D28: Requests for code varied by assignment, while requests for explanation stayed steady
